title: KV adaptive warmup and thrashing tests
content:
Purpose / quick summary:
This is an exploratory scratchpad for experiments that measure KV miss penalty and the trade-offs for background prefetch / warmup strategies. Goal: quantify when prefetch helps (reduced token latency + higher reuse) vs when it hurts (memory BW saturation, added latency for cold batches, thrashing).

Background / motivation:
- We've tuned eviction heuristics for steady hotsets, but we still see tail latency regressions on bursty traffic where many requests reference fresh prefixes.
- Prefetching frequently-candidate KV blocks ahead of time is attractive (reduce first-request miss penalty), but it uses memory bandwidth and can increase contention for GPU DRAM when aggressive.
- Need an adaptively gated approach: prefetch when expected benefit > bandwidth/latency cost.

Hypotheses:
1) Small, targeted prefetch (prefetch-depth 2-4 entries for sampled hot prefixes) reduces 95th token latency by 10-25% on bursty traces without increasing average latency.
2) Aggressive blanket prefetch (depth >= 8, on every new prefix) increases memory writes/reads and causes >10% tail regressions on models with long KV vectors due to memory-bandwidth saturation.
3) An occupancy-aware prefetch gate (samples hotness + current BW util) can capture most wins and avoid thrashing.

Experiment design:
- Workloads: three synthetic traces + one production-ish trace (sampled anonymized prefixes from recent hosted traffic - low-privacy dump).
  * bursty_short: many new prefixes, sequence length 64, batch=16, 90% short L1 hotset.
  * stable_hotset: repeated same hot prefixes, sequence length 128, batch=32.
  * mixed_skew: zipfian access to 10k keys, sequences 32-256 variable.
  * prod_sample_202501 (anonymized): 10k requests sampled over 30 min.
- Metrics:
  * miss_rate (per-request KV miss)
  * miss_penalty_ms (time difference for request where KV miss occurs vs hit)
  * token_latency_p50/p95/p99
  * host-side GPU DRAM BW util (perf counter) as percent
  * background_prefetch_bytes/sec
  * CPU overhead for prefetch task
- Configs tested:
  A) baseline - no prefetch, LRU eviction
  B) heuristic-prefetch (prefix-frequency > threshold => prefetch depth=3)
  C) aggressive-prefetch (depth=8, prefetch for any unseen prefix)
  D) adaptive-prefetch (gate: sample hotness + if memory_bw < 60% allow; dynamic depth 1-4)
  E) occupancy-conservative (only prefetch when cache occupancy < 70%)

Microbench tooling / commands used (local bench harness):
- bench script: infra/bench/bench_kv.py (instrumented)
- sample command: python infra/bench/bench_kv.py --trace traces/bursty_short.json --model gptx-small --batch 16 --seq 64 --config configs/prefetch_depth=3 --profile perf --out results/bursty_depth3.json
- perf collection: nv-nsight and perf counters collected with run_prof.sh wrapper.

Key numeric snapshots (representative; avg over 5 runs):
- bursty_short (batch=16, seq=64):
  * Baseline: miss_rate=0.37, miss_penalty_ms=14.6, token_p95=92ms, gpu_bw=42%
  * Heuristic-prefetch (depth=3): miss_rate=0.18, miss_penalty_ms=6.3, token_p95=72ms, gpu_bw=49%, prefetch_bytes/s=120MB/s
  * Aggressive (depth=8): miss_rate=0.09, miss_penalty_ms=3.9, token_p95=86ms, gpu_bw=78%, prefetch_bytes/s=410MB/s (note tail worsened vs heuristic)
  * Adaptive (gate at 60% BW): miss_rate=0.14, miss_penalty_ms=5.1, token_p95=70ms, gpu_bw=55%

- mixed_skew (zipf, batch=24):
  * Baseline: miss_rate=0.21, token_p95=110ms, gpu_bw=36%
  * Aggressive: miss_rate=0.06, token_p95=122ms, gpu_bw=64% (bandwidth increase dominates)
  * Adaptive: miss_rate=0.11, token_p95=104ms, gpu_bw=48%

Interpretation / takeaways:
- Prefetch reduces miss penalty significantly for bursty workloads and improves tail latency up to a point. But the wins saturate and reversing occurs when memory bandwidth approaches ~70% on our test machines.
- Depth tuning matters: depth 3 is often a sweet spot; depth 8 gives diminishing returns on miss_rate but increases BW and sometimes tail latency.
- Adaptive gating that uses a lightweight BW signal + simple hotness sampling recovers most of the wins of aggressive prefetch without the bandwidth penalty.
- Cache occupancy alone is not a sufficient signal (we saw cases where occupancy < 70% but BW still spiked because many large KV vectors were in flight).

Profiling notes (what we saw with nvprof/perf):
- Background prefetch shows up as large sustained DRAM read streams during request bursts.
- Kernel-level stalls increased on some configurations: memcpy and kernel dispatch contention — need to look at prioritized prefetch scheduling.
- CPU worker queues: prefetch tasks occasionally starved KV-lookup threads when prefetch thread priority was equal. We should lower prefetch thread niceness.

Proposed pragmatic policy (sketch):
1) Light sampling: on first-seen prefix, do an async sample request to check hotness (track frequency in tiny LRU sketch), only trigger prefetch if freq > f_threshold within a short window (e.g., 30s).
2) Prefetch depth: choose depth = min(4, 1 + floor(log2(freq_estimate))) capped by model-dependent KV vector size budget.
3) BW gate: query coarse GPU BW util emitter (every 200ms); if BW > 65% reduce prefetch depth to 0 or delay window.
4) Priority: schedule prefetch tasks at lower CPU/gpu priority; prefetch should yield to active request lookups.
5) Safety fallback: if eviction churn increases > X% (measured by eviction rate and re-fetch within Y seconds), automatically back off prefetch aggressiveness.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need to measure impact on cost (prefetch bytes -> billing/egress) for Dedicated customers with metered GPUs.
- Evaluate interaction with KV quantization (smaller KV vectors may shift BW thresholds - need cross-product tests).
- Could we leverage the routing layer to pre-warm particular model replicas during expected bursts (predictive warmup)? Tie into autoscaler signals.
- Implement a lightweight BW emitter in runtime: options are GPU perf counters, or local controller estimating DRAM throughput via nvml.
- Need A/B run in staging against real prod_sample_202501 to validate non-regression.

Next steps / action items:
- <@Liam> prototype BW emitter (blocked on access to cuda perf counters in k8s); ask infra for permission to install driver agent. (ETA: 1 week)
- <@Marta> add a prefetch thread niceness change and rerun mixed_skew tests. (ETA: 3 days)
- <@Devon> implement the adaptive gate logic in bench harness (simple rule engine) and add logging for eviction churn. (ETA: 1 week)
- Schedule a two-hour sync to review staging A/B runs: propose Tue 2025-02-10 10:00 PST.

Appendix: small sample of commands and small parse script used to summarize results:
- python infra/bench/bench_kv.py --trace traces/prod_sample_202501.json --batch 32 --seq 128 --config prefetch_mode=adaptive --profile perf --runs 5 --out out/prod_adaptive.json
- quick stats: python infra/bench/parse_results.py out/prod_adaptive.json --metrics miss_rate,miss_penalty_ms,token_p95,gpu_bw --csv

Notes to self (rough):
- Watch for correlation between large sequence lengths (>=256) and BW spike impact. Long sequences => larger KV vectors = heavier prefetch cost.
- Consider slotting prefetch into idle GPU cycles (post-token generation padding) if we can detect slack.
- Add unit tests for gate logic (simulate BW values, hotness counters).

References / related tickets:
- RWD-1023 (prefetch research epic)
- runtime PR #1287 (bench harness updates, new perf hooks)

End of doc.
